purpose: Fedratinib is used to treat a bone marrow disease called myelofibrosis, which causes abnormal blood cell production and scarring of the bone marrow. It can be used in adults who are newly diagnosed or whose disease has come back or stopped responding to another similar medication called ruxolitinib. It helps reduce an enlarged spleen and relieve symptoms like fatigue, night sweats, and bone pain.
how_it_works: Your body has certain proteins called JAK2 that send signals telling cells to grow and multiply. In myelofibrosis, these signals go haywire and cause too many abnormal cells to be made. Fedratinib works by blocking JAK2, essentially turning down those overactive signals so the disease is better controlled and your symptoms improve.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are very common, especially when you first start. You may also feel more tired than usual, have muscle aches, or notice swelling in your legs or feet. Some people have changes in their blood counts, such as low red blood cells (anemia) or low platelets. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to monitor these.
warnings: The most serious warning is a rare but dangerous brain condition called Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is caused by low thiamine (vitamin B1) levels. You will need your thiamine levels checked before and during treatment, and you may need to take vitamin B1 supplements. Tell your doctor right away if you feel confused, have trouble walking, or notice vision changes. This medicine can also lower your blood counts, raising your risk of infection or bleeding, so report any fever, unusual bruising, or bleeding promptly. It should not be used during pregnancy as it can harm an unborn baby.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 400 mg taken by mouth once a day with food. Taking it with food helps reduce stomach upset and nausea. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have kidney or liver problems or if you experience certain side effects. Always take it at the same time each day and never stop without talking to your doctor first.
